title: Feedback that changes behaviour

audience.who: corporate employees who give feedback to peers or to people they lead, in one-to-ones and everyday work
audience.knows: feedback often feels awkward, and sometimes the same thing happens again the next week
audience.cares_about: the other person actually doing something differently next time, without damaging the working relationship

outcome: In their next piece of feedback, the viewer names one specific, observed behaviour and its impact, then asks a question and agrees one next step, so the other person knows exactly what to repeat or change
through_line: Feedback changes behaviour when it points at a specific action the person can repeat or change, says what it caused, and ends in a shared next step; a verdict about the person only changes how they feel

arc_plan.what: Framed as invented: a teammate tells you only on the due day that a deliverable will be late. You say 'you need to be more proactive'. They nod, feel bad, and two weeks later it happens again, because nothing told them what to do differently.
What the viewer leaves able to do: turn a verdict like 'be more proactive' into feedback the other person can act on next time
The shape, in order, applied to the same moment: the specific behaviour you saw (when and what, not a trait), its concrete impact, then a question that hears their side and agrees one next step
Two lines about the same late deliverable, one a judgement of the person, one naming behaviour and impact; the viewer decides which one gives the teammate something to do differently
Back to the opening: the same moment, now with the shape; the teammate proposes a next step, and the next slip gets flagged early

must_cover.what: name a specific, observed behaviour rather than a trait or a judgement of the person
say the concrete impact of that behaviour
end with a question that invites their view and agrees a next step, so it becomes a conversation, not a verdict
why vague or person-directed feedback tends to change feelings but not the next action
the shape presented as common workplace practice, never as a named research finding unless the knowledge sheet grounds a specific attributable source

must_avoid: statistics or research citations the knowledge sheet does not ground with a real, named source
learning-styles or other debunked pop-psychology claims, including the 'feedback sandwich' presented as best practice
invented lines attributed to a real study or person
a list of generic feedback tips instead of the one running example
'in this video we will' or any agenda slide
a trivia question in place of a real decision the viewer could face
the teammate shown as lazy or incompetent; the slip is ordinary
HR, disciplinary or formal performance-review procedure
a real company or a real named person
example_posture: One invented, ordinary moment (a deliverable flagged late on the due day) between two generic colleagues, framed as illustrative, shown broken at the start and fixed at the end; no real company, no industry jargon
visual_direction: A presenter figure for the opening question and the close; inside, the one running moment between two illustrated colleagues, with their faces showing how each line lands; the shape built up as a short sequence of three marks that stays on screen and returns at the check and payoff; a clear before and after between the verdict and the specific ask, with a calendar or deadline the viewer can read
voice_note: A mentor who has given plenty of feedback that did not land before learning the shape; plain, warm, direct, a colleague not a coach; say each point once and let the picture carry the rest
open_questions: No source document was supplied; the shape relies on the knowledge sheet grounding a recognised workplace practice (behaviour, impact, question or next step), not a company policy
Two minutes is tight for the full teaching arc; bridge and apply are folded into build and payoff
